title.en: Why are you here? Um … zu

summary.en: Explain a purpose and recognize why the final action comes last.

body.en:
**Ich bin hier, um Geld zu verdienen.** — “I’m here to earn money.” The construction **um … zu + infinitive** states a purpose. *Um* opens the purpose part, and *zu* appears before the final action word: *um Geld zu verdienen*. The object, *Geld*, comes before that final pair.

The understood person is the same in both parts: Titus is here, and Titus intends to earn. For this sort of shared-person purpose, German does not need to repeat *ich* after *um*. When the person changes, a clause with *damit* can state the purpose instead: *Ich arbeite, damit du studieren kannst.* — “I work so that you can study.”

**Aber ich bin nicht hier, um Freunde zu finden.** — “But I’m not here to make friends.” *Aber* marks the contrast without changing the ordinary order of the following main clause. *Freunde finden* is literally “find friends”; idiomatic English normally says “make friends”. Do not translate *finden* as “make” everywhere: *einen Schlüssel finden* means finding a key.

Keep the small words separate in the word drawer. Here *um* signals purpose and *zu* marks an infinitive. Their other uses are different: *um den Laden* can mean “around the shop”, while *zu einer Freundin* means “to a female friend” and takes the dative. Neither of those spatial meanings belongs in the purpose sentence.

A new practice sentence is *Ich komme, um dich zu sehen.* — “I’m coming to see you.” First locate the shared person, then listen for the action after *zu*.
